Name: subgoal_schedule_myopia
Title: Solving the Wrong Subgoal First: Overthinking as a Dependency-Scheduling Failure in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: A problem's subgoals form a dependency DAG whose prerequisites impose a partial order; reasoning models schedule subgoals myopically rather than dependency-respectingly, frequently attacking a subgoal before its prerequisites are established. This premature scheduling wastes tokens on flailing and re-derivation. The model already carries an internal, decodable 'prerequisite-readiness' signal at each subgoal-onset that it fails to consult, and steering generation toward dependency-respecting order cuts tokens without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Probing work shows LLM hidden states encode reasoning-DAG geometry (From Chains to DAGs, 2026) and that models are largely myopic/incremental planners with weak global planning (No Global Plan in CoT, 2026; Internal Planning: Horizon and Branch Awareness, 2025; Detecting and Characterizing Planning, 2025). Efficiency work characterizes overthinking as an inverted-U length effect (When More is Less, 2025) or as decorative/redundant steps (Thought Anchors; TTS). A shortest-path study shows next-token predictors are biased toward systematically inefficient (backtracking) traces (2025). Crucially, none connect the problem's *dependency structure* to *compute waste*: no prior work identifies suboptimal subgoal *ordering* (attacking a subgoal before its prerequisites) as a distinct, quantifiable source of overthinking, nor tests whether a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal governs it, nor intervenes on scheduling to save compute. This differs from my prior proposals (which target stopping, verification, length priors, and framing effects) by targeting the *order* in which reasoning is performed. It also goes beyond DAG-probing (which is diagnostic and static) by tying the encoded DAG to a behavioral scheduling failure and a causal efficiency intervention.
Abstract: Reasoning models overthink, but the role of *ordering* in that waste is unexamined. Many problems decompose into subgoals with prerequisite dependencies—a directed acyclic graph whose topological orders are the valid schedules. We hypothesize that reasoning models schedule subgoals myopically: they frequently begin a subgoal before its prerequisites are established, then flail or re-derive, spending tokens that a dependency-respecting order would avoid. We further hypothesize the model already encodes, at each subgoal onset, a prerequisite-readiness signal (are the inputs this subgoal needs already available in context?) that it does not act on. Using multi-step problems with recoverable dependency structure (GSM8K, MATH500, and templated multi-constraint word/logic problems where we can annotate a ground-truth subgoal DAG) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) segment traces into subgoals, align them to DAG nodes, and measure a scheduling-inversion rate (subgoals started before their prerequisites) and its token cost via truncate-and-resume and re-derivation detection; (2) show inversions predict wasted tokens beyond length or decorative-step baselines; (3) train a linear probe at subgoal onset to decode prerequisite-readiness and test its separability from a generic difficulty/confidence probe; (4) causally validate via activation patching—patching a high-readiness state into a premature-onset context should shift the model to a ready subgoal; and (5) deploy a training-free scheduling steer that, when readiness is low, nudges the model to defer the premature subgoal, cutting tokens at equal accuracy versus length-aware and reactive-pruning baselines. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as a dependency-scheduling failure with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted. The subgoal DAG and trace-to-node alignment are shared infrastructure: templated multi-constraint word problems and small logic/scheduling puzzles have a DAG known by construction; for GSM8K and MATH500 we annotate the subgoal DAG by solution parsing plus LLM-judge, human-validated on a 100-item spot-check (inter-annotator/judge agreement reported). Traces are segmented into subgoals at step delimiters and each subgoal is aligned to a DAG node by semantic matching plus LLM-judge; a scheduling-inversion = a subgoal begun before all its prerequisite nodes were established earlier in the trace.

Experiment 1 (H1 - reasoning models commit scheduling inversions rather than respecting the dependency order): Tests whether models frequently begin subgoals before their prerequisites are established. Data: constructed and adapted - 300 templated multi-constraint word problems and 200 logic/scheduling puzzles built with known DAGs (varying width/depth), plus 400 GSM8K and 300 MATH500 problems with annotated DAGs; these counts give enough multi-subgoal traces while keeping per-trace segmentation/alignment affordable. Systems compared: the observed per-trace inversion rate against a random-scheduling null (the inversion rate expected if subgoals were ordered uniformly at random among the DAG's topological-order violations), across datasets and the four model sizes. Decisive metric: per-trace scheduling-inversion rate, first; reported against the random-scheduling null and against the ideal (zero-inversion) schedule. Convincing: the observed inversion rate is substantial (>= 15% of subgoal onsets are inversions) and significantly above zero, but below the random-null (models are partly, not fully, dependency-respecting), consistent across datasets. Indecision band: an inversion rate of 5-15% is a weak phenomenon reported as such and does not strongly motivate the intervention. Negative result: an inversion rate < 5% (models already schedule near-optimally) refutes H1 and removes the premise for the remaining experiments; an inversion rate at or above the random null would instead indicate alignment failure rather than a real scheduling signal and triggers an alignment audit.

Experiment 2 (H2 - inversions cause wasted tokens through flailing and re-derivation): Tests whether inversions predict wasted compute beyond length and decorative-step baselines. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. For each inversion we measure downstream waste via (a) truncate-and-resume estimating the minimal-solve length under a forced dependency-respecting order (prerequisite subgoals prompted first) on a 200-problem subsample, (b) re-derivation detection (value-producing statements re-derived after a premature attempt), and (c) dead-end/backtrack detection. We then regress per-trace wasted tokens on inversion rate versus baselines: trace length, decorative-step fraction, and a difficulty probe. Systems compared: inversion-rate predictor vs each baseline predictor. Decisive metric: held-out incremental R2 of inversion rate for predicting wasted tokens over the strongest baseline, first; plus the mean wasted tokens attributable to a single inversion. Convincing: inversion rate adds >= 0.05 R2 over the best baseline (significant), and forcing a dependency-respecting order reduces minimal-solve length by >= 15% on the subsample. Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or a 5-15% forced-order reduction, is partial support. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02 and < 5% forced-order reduction means inversions do not cause measurable waste, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal exists at subgoal onset and is separable from difficulty/confidence): Tests whether the residual stream at subgoal onset encodes whether the upcoming subgoal's prerequisites are satisfied, distinct from generic difficulty/confidence. Data: subgoal-onset activations (before the subgoal is generated) from Experiment 1 traces, labeled by DAG alignment as prerequisites-satisfied vs not, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: a linear readiness probe (target = prerequisites satisfied), a difficulty probe (pass-rate), and a confidence probe. Systems compared: readiness probe vs difficulty/confidence probes; principal angles among their directions and joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the readiness probe, first; plus its principal angle to the difficulty and confidence directions. Convincing: readiness AUROC >= 0.7 at the best layer, the readiness direction not collinear with difficulty or confidence (angle >= 30 degrees to each), adding significant R2 over both - establishing that readiness is decodable even at onsets the model then treats as inversions (an unconsulted signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.7, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: AUROC < 0.6, or collinearity with difficulty/confidence (angle < 20 degrees), means there is no distinct readiness signal, refuting H3.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal - patching readiness redirects the model to a ready subgoal): Tests whether the readiness representation causally governs which subgoal is attacked. Data: 150 premature-onset contexts (subset of Experiment 1) where a dependency-ready subgoal is also available; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention: patch a high-readiness state (from a context where a ready subgoal is available) into the premature-onset context at the Experiment-3 layer and test whether the model switches to a dependency-ready subgoal (inversion avoided, tokens dropped). Controls: matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems preserved. Systems compared: real readiness patch vs random-direction control vs no intervention. Decisive metric: fraction of premature onsets redirected to a dependency-ready subgoal under patching, first; secondary token reduction, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: real patching redirects >= 50% of premature onsets and reduces tokens while the random control redirects < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: a 20-50% redirection, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% redirection or the random control matching the real direction means readiness is correlational not causal, refuting H3's causal reading.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a scheduling steer cuts tokens at equal accuracy): Tests the training-free intervention. Data: full templated set (300), puzzles (200), GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 sample (300) on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B-subsample replications). Online, at each subgoal onset the readiness probe is read; when it predicts low readiness (an impending inversion), a steer is applied - steering along the readiness direction, or injecting a terse 'first establish prerequisites' cue - to defer the premature subgoal. Systems compared: scheduling steer vs no intervention vs length-aware filtering vs reactive pruning vs decorative-step skipping vs fixed truncation. Decisive metric: token reduction at matched accuracy (accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention), first; secondary inversion-rate reduction and wall-clock speedup, on overall and hardest strata. Convincing: the scheduling steer cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 15% within 1 point of baseline accuracy and beats the length-aware and reactive-pruning baselines at matched accuracy, with a measurable inversion-rate drop. Indecision band: a 5-15% token reduction, or parity with (not beating) the strongest baseline, is a marginal result. Negative result: < 5% reduction or > 2 point accuracy loss means scheduling steering is not an efficiency win, refuting H4.

Experiment 6 (H4 specificity and generalization - beneficial-exploration guard and transfer): Tests that suppressing inversions does not remove genuinely useful exploration, and whether probe/steer transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 5 runs plus a hand-labeled subset where an apparent inversion is beneficial exploration (the model probes a subgoal to discover its prerequisites). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived readiness probe and steer to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; correlate inversion rate with DAG width/depth. Systems compared: steer with vs without the beneficial-exploration guard threshold; in-model vs transferred probe/steer; low- vs high-width/depth DAGs. Decisive metric: accuracy on beneficial-exploration items under the guarded steer, first; plus transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-model and the inversion-rate/DAG-complexity correlation. Convincing: the guarded steer preserves beneficial-exploration accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention while still cutting tokens elsewhere, transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model AUROC, and inversion rate rises with DAG width/depth. Indecision band: transferred AUROC 40-70% of in-model, or a beneficial-exploration accuracy loss of 1-3 points, is weak/partial. Negative result: the guard failing to protect beneficial exploration (> 3 point loss) or transferred AUROC < 40% means the intervention is unsafe or idiosyncratic, bounding H4's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Annotating a ground-truth subgoal DAG for open math is noisy; we anchor the strongest claims on templated problems and puzzles with known structure, using GSM8K/MATH500 as corroboration with human-validated annotations. Aligning generated subgoals to DAG nodes is imperfect; we use semantic matching + LLM-judge with agreement reporting. Some scheduling 'inversions' may be legitimate exploration (probing a subgoal to learn its prerequisites), so suppressing them could hurt accuracy; the failure analysis and steer thresholds explicitly guard this, and finding that inversions are largely beneficial would be an informative negative result. The readiness signal may be inseparable from generic difficulty/confidence, weakening the mechanistic framing; the separability analysis and causal patching address this. Steering could push activations off-distribution and introduce errors; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Intervention gains may not exceed strong length-aware or pruning baselines, but the scheduling-failure diagnosis (a named, quantifiable, dependency-structured source of overthinking) is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.
